### A

The following discussion concerns an invented novel, The City Without Clocks, by an equally imaginary writer, Mina Vale. Its setting is a town whose public clocks stop during a dispute over their management. The novel's interest lies elsewhere: inhabitants continue to measure time, but disagree over whose measurements should organise shared activities. No acquaintance with another book is required to follow the argument. The incidents and competing interpretations needed for this reading are presented in the discussion itself.

### B

The narrator is a baker who assembles his account after the dispute has ended. Although his chapters carry dates, they are not daily diary entries written at those dates. He sometimes places a later conversation beside an earlier event to explain what he eventually came to understand. This arrangement gives the narrative an appearance of immediate observation while retaining the advantages and distortions of hindsight.

### C

The clocks do not stop because everyone has lost the ability to repair them. The committee controlling their cases refuses access to the mechanisms until its authority is recognised. Meanwhile, households continue to use watches, shadows and private routines. Public silence is consequently an exercise of control, not the disappearance of measurement. The baker initially describes a town released from the clock, then notices that only some inhabitants possess convenient alternatives. What sounds like freedom in his first description can also be read as an unequal distribution of practical resources.

### D

A watchmaker is especially irritated by the baker's account. He sees his workshop described as empty during a week when he remembers working late. Their disagreement is not resolved by a surviving photograph: that image shows an empty room but carries no reliable date. The incident exposes the weakness of using one attractive piece of evidence to settle a question it cannot answer. It also prevents readers from treating the baker's position as an observer as a guarantee of accuracy.

### E

The ferry chapter shifts attention from clocks to information. A clerk possesses the only written timetable and announces departures according to a private notebook. Passengers cannot check whether a missed crossing reflects their lateness or a change he has made. Restoring a working clock would not, by itself, make his decisions transparent. The chapter places control over a shared schedule alongside control over a mechanism. Both may shape other people's opportunities, although they do so through different means. The dispute about time has therefore extended beyond the original locked clock cases.

### F

In a winter scene, children carry small watches to a public gathering and compare their readings. The scene is often the most cheerful part of a retelling of the plot. Yet the watches disagree, and the adults cannot decide which one should determine when the gathering begins. It shows that having many measurements leaves a further collective decision to make.

### G

Halfway through his account, the baker revises his explanation of an argument with a neighbour. At first he had claimed that she ignored their agreed meeting time. He later admits that he had told her a different time from the one he had written in his own notebook. An appendix preserves the earlier description beside the revision. It makes visible a habit of assigning responsibility to someone else before checking his own contribution. The preserved first version lets readers inspect that change.

### H

One morning, a school opens later than planned because its staff receive conflicting messages about the start time. A local hero subsequently claims that his speech has solved the town's difficulties when the school resumes its usual hours. The novel supplies a narrower explanation: two teachers had compared the messages and issued a single corrected notice. Their action addresses that particular confusion. It does not demonstrate that the hero's broader political programme has succeeded, nor that every household now accepts the same schedule. The narrative separates a visible improvement from the ambitious explanation attached to it.

### I

A bell recurs at several moments, first at a wedding and later during a funeral. Its notes are described in nearly identical words, but the people listening respond differently. The repetition prevents the sound from carrying one fixed emotional meaning throughout the book. It also asks readers to attend to the surrounding activity, rather than to treat a recurring object as a code with a single translation. The bell remains recognisable while its role changes. Continuity of description and continuity of significance are thus deliberately pulled apart.

### J

Two fictional reviewers illustrate the disagreement the ending can provoke. Hale calls the book nostalgic, arguing that neighbours eventually rediscover ways of cooperating without elaborate public machinery. Ruan reads the same scenes as a warning about the unpaid labour required to make such cooperation possible. Both refer to the baker's final description of a shared meal. The disagreement cannot be explained simply by saying that they noticed different plot events.

### K

These readings should not be confused with statements by the novelist about how an actual town ought to be governed. The baker, the watchmaker and the reviewers occupy distinguishable positions in the discussion. A claim made confidently by one of them is not automatically endorsed by the narrative as a whole. This distinction matters particularly when a character promises that a single change will benefit everyone. The novel frequently allows that promise to stand beside an incident that makes it harder to accept without qualification.

### L

In the final chapters, the public clocks remain unrepaired. Some activities follow a collectively posted timetable; others depend on private arrangements. The shared meal takes place, but participants still disagree about which day should count as the town's anniversary. The ending therefore demonstrates an instance of cooperation rather than a complete settlement. Readers are given enough to recognise an achievement, while the unresolved disagreement prevents that achievement from becoming a guarantee that the town's new arrangements will remain stable.

### M

The discussion of the meal also contains an easily missed typographical distinction. Words from an official notice are printed in capitals; the baker's later comments appear in ordinary type. The difference identifies who is speaking at that point, rather than signalling that one statement is more truthful. Here the notice reads “MEET AT THE HALL”; the baker adds that several neighbours first went to the garden. Both pieces of information belong to the scene.

### N

Near the close, the baker calls the dispute a six-month interruption, even though the dates printed at the beginning and end span a longer period. The discussion does not invite readers to calculate a corrected duration from outside information. It identifies what the discrepancy makes visible: his summary excludes the earlier weeks when only a few workers were affected. For him, the disruption begins when it enters his own routine. The apparent numerical inconsistency becomes part of a question about perspective, rather than being silently repaired into a neutral timeline.

### O

Reading the novel as an uncomplicated rejection of clocks would consequently overlook much of its argument. Devices, records, memories and public agreements all matter, but none can be substituted for all the others. The stopped clocks make certain relationships easier to see; they do not create every conflict that emerges. The book leaves readers considering whose inconvenience becomes publicly recognisable, whose work supports a shared arrangement and how a narrator's later explanation reshapes an event. Those questions remain available precisely because the final meal has not been made to settle everything.
